verses.text: Then Yahweh said to me, “Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my mind would not be toward this people. Cast them out of my sight, and let them go out!

It shall happen, when they tell you, ‘Where shall we go out?’ Then you shall tell them, ‘Yahweh says: “Such as are for death, to death; and such as are for the sword, to the sword; and such as are for the famine, to the famine; and such as are for captivity, to captivity.”’
“I will appoint over them four kinds,” says Yahweh: “the sword to kill, and the dogs to tear, and the birds of the sky, and the animals of the earth, to devour and to destroy.
I will cause them to be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh, the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, for that which he did in Jerusalem.
For who will have pity on you, Jerusalem? or who will bemoan you? or who will turn aside to ask of your welfare?
You have rejected me,” says Yahweh. “You have gone backward: therefore I have stretched out my hand against you, and destroyed you; I am weary with repenting.
I have winnowed them with a fan in the gates of the land; I have bereaved them of children. I have destroyed my people. They didn’t return from their ways.

Their widows are increased to me above the sand of the seas; I have brought on them against the mother of the young men a destroyer at noonday. I have caused anguish and terrors to fall on her suddenly.

She who has borne seven languishes; she has given up the spirit. Her sun has gone down while it was yet day. She has been disappointed and confounded: and their residue will I deliver to the sword before their enemies,” says Yahweh.
Woe is me, my mother, that you have borne me a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole earth! I have not lent, neither have men lent to me; yet everyone of them curses me.
Yahweh said, “Most certainly I will strengthen you for good. Most certainly I will cause the enemy to make supplication to you in the time of evil and in the time of affliction.
Can one break iron, even iron from the north, and brass?
Your substance and your treasures will I give for a plunder without price, and that for all your sins, even in all your borders.
I will make them to pass with your enemies into a land which you don’t know; for a fire is kindled in my anger, which shall burn on you.”
Yahweh, you know; remember me, and visit me, and avenge me of my persecutors. You are patient, so don’t take me away. Know that for your sake I have suffered reproach.
Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words were to me a joy and the rejoicing of my heart, for I am called by your name, Yahweh, God of Armies.
I didn’t sit in the assembly of those who make merry, nor rejoiced; I sat alone because of your hand; for you have filled me with indignation.
Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuses to be healed? Will you indeed be to me as a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?

Therefore Yahweh says, “If you return, then I will bring you again, that you may stand before me; and if you take out the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth. They shall return to you, but you shall not return to them.
I will make you to this people a fortified bronze wall; and they shall fight against you, but they shall not prevail against you; for I am with you to save you and to deliver you,” says Yahweh.
“I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and I will redeem you out of the hand of the terrible.”

footnotes.content: Even Moses and Samuel—men of such power before God—couldn't turn His heart when a people had wandered too far. This tells us that prayer's strength lies not in the praying one, but in the people's own returning. Sometimes the only mercy left is to let go and learn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord sorts out fates with terrible clarity: death to those destined for death, the sword for those the sword will claim. It sounds harsh until you've lived long enough to see His mercy in an ending that comes swift rather than prolonged in misery.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four agents of judgment—sword, dogs, birds, wild beasts—named plainly. The Lord doesn't hide the cost of rejection. Yet even in this harshness, there's a strange mercy: an end, not an endless twilight of half-life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Manasseh's name carries the weight here—a king who once led Judah astray, and even his later repentance couldn't undo the kingdoms' long memory of his evil. We see how one person's turning from God ripples across generations. Yet Manasseh himself repented; the Lord sees that too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jerusalem cries out: Who will pity me? The answer—no one—stings, but only until we understand it. When we've emptied ourselves of the Lord, we have emptied ourselves of the only pity worth having. No human can fill that well.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You have rejected me," He says, and His own weariness enters the verse—weary with repenting. Even God grieves when His outstretched hand is refused again and again. There's profound sorrow in a parent who must finally let a child go.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The winnowing fan at the gates—separating chaff from grain, separating those who will return from those locked in their own stubbornness. The Lord's grief deepens: "I have destroyed my people," and yet they still won't turn. That refusal is the deepest wound.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The widow count rises like sand; a destroyer strikes at noonday, when women gather with their young. The imagery is stark—terror made visible. In a long life, you learn that judgment always has a human face, always a mother weeping.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The mother who bore seven—a traditional symbol of fullness—now languishes as her sun goes down at midday, her hopes shattered. Yet even here, the Lord speaks of what remains: a residue delivered to the sword. Judgment, but not annihilation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah's lament is almost violent in its honesty: "Woe is me." He didn't borrow or lend—he stayed clean—yet everyone curses him. The righteous often find themselves standing alone, paying a price for fidelity. He's crying out what many faithful ones feel but rarely speak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here the pivot: "Most certainly I will strengthen you." The Lord answers Jeremiah's despair not with false comfort but with His own commitment—a turning point. Notice He promises strength, not escape. That's the answer that sustains prophets: not removal from the furnace, but presence within it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Can one break iron, even iron from the north?" Iron from the north speaks of Babylon's empire—overwhelming might. The question hangs unanswered until Jeremiah remembers: the Lord is mightier than northern iron. Not by human strength, but by His unbreakable word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Treasures given for plunder without price—the thing of value becomes worthless spoil. This is how exile works: what you labored for becomes a slave's pittance. Yet the Lord lists this plainly, as though to say: I see the cost. I know what you're losing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Driven into a land unknown, fire burning with His anger—exile is displacement and terror. Yet even this word comes from the Lord's mouth with clarity, not ambush. Judgment announced is judgment that carries a strange grace: you can prepare your heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah pleads: "Remember me, visit me, avenge me." He's suffered reproach for God's sake, and he's asking—almost demanding—that the Lord see it. There's courage in bringing your complaint before God. He'd rather hear your raw truth than your practiced prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Your words were found, and I ate them." Jeremiah ate God's word as food—the only nourishment that held him. Note the echoing: he who tasted God's words as joy will soon carry them as burden. To consume the Lord's word is to take in both feast and fire.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He sat alone, not in merrymaking but in indignation—filled by God's hand. The prophet's loneliness isn't failure; it's the mark of one called to stand apart and see what others refuse. In solitude, God's word deepens its grip.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Why is my pain perpetual?" Jeremiah accuses God of being like a deceitful brook—waters that fail when you need them most. It's a raw question, almost a betrayal of trust. The Lord doesn't silence him; He lets the question stand and answers through presence, not explanation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If you return, then I will bring you again." The condition isn't about Jeremiah's city but his own heart—to separate precious from vile in himself, to let the Lord use his mouth. The promise: they will seek you, but you will not return to them. Standing before God means standing alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will make you a fortified bronze wall." Bronze—ancient symbol of strength and endurance. Not escape from battle, but transformation into a wall that cannot be breached. The Lord's promise isn't safety from opposition; it's unshakeable standing within it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and I will redeem you out of the hand of the terrible." Readers today hear an echo in these words: the Lord's redemption isn't about ease or escape, but about His faithfulness to snatch us from what would destroy us. After long years, we know this promise holds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
